title: Week 4: Persistent homology
section: Homology at many scales is not enough
text:
Homology at many scales is not enough
A list of Betti numbers tells us how many classes exist.
It does not tell us which earlier classes survived.
Lecture walkthrough

title: Week 4: Persistent homology
text:
From filtration to memory
Week 3 used the A, B and C example to motivate multiple resolutions and built the nested family
\[K_0\subseteq K_1\subseteq\cdots.\]
Week 4 asks what the nested complexes alone do not tell us: which earlier homology class became which later class?

title: Week 4: Persistent homology
text:
Inclusion creates memory
\[K_i\hookrightarrow K_j\]
means every simplex of \(K_i\) is also in \(K_j\).
\(K_j\) may contain additional simplices; the old simplices do not grow.
induces
\[H_p(K_i;\mathbb F)\xrightarrow{(\iota_{i,j})_*}H_p(K_j;\mathbb F).\]
The maps are the memory.

title: Week 4: Persistent homology
section: Inclusion of complexes, not necessarily of homology
text:
Inclusion of complexes, not necessarily of homology
Outline triangle \(\hookrightarrow\) filled triangle.
The edge cycle remains as a chain. It becomes the boundary of the new face:
\[[z]\longmapsto0.\]

▶ Likely sticking point. The induced map on homology need not be injective.

title: Week 4: Persistent homology
section: Component merging is also a map
text:
Component merging is also a map
Before: \(H_0\cong\mathbb F_2^2=\langle e_1,e_2\rangle\).
After:
\[e_1\mapsto e,\qquad e_2\mapsto e.\]
The direction \(e_1+e_2\) is killed.

title: Week 4: Persistent homology
text:
Persistence module
\[V_i=H_p(K_i;\mathbb F),\qquad\varphi_{i,j}=(\iota_{i,j})_*.\]
\[\varphi_{j,k}\varphi_{i,j}=\varphi_{i,k}.\]

◇ Object check. The module is every vector space and every compatible map, not merely the Betti numbers.

title: Week 4: Persistent homology
text:
One interval, one idealised lifetime
\[I[b,d)_a=\begin{cases}\mathbb F,&b\leq a<d,\\0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}\]
For suitable one-parameter modules:
\[V\cong\bigoplus_\ell I[b_\ell,d_\ell).\]

title: Week 4: Persistent homology
text:
Module, barcode, diagram
Persistence module: spaces and maps.
Barcode: interval summands.
Diagram: birth-death points.
Closely related, but not the same object by definition.

title: Week 4: Persistent homology
text:
What matrix reduction pairs
Order simplices compatibly with the filtration.
Reduce the boundary matrix over \(\mathbb F_2\).
Lowest 1 + column index \(\longrightarrow\) birth-death pair.
Unpaired birth \(\longrightarrow\) essential within the computed range.

title: Week 4: Persistent homology
text:
One triangle, one complete story

Vertices \(\to\) component births.
Connecting edges \(\to\) component deaths.
Final edge \(\to\) one-cycle birth.
Triangular face \(\to\) one-cycle death.
Matrix pairings \(\to\) barcode intervals.

title: Week 4: Persistent homology
text:
Return to the house

At the first edge stage, the outer cycle is \(c\). Adding the roof-base edge splits our convenient description into the roof cycle \(r\) and room cycle \(q\):
\[c=r+q.\]
Filling the roof sends \([r]\mapsto0\) while \([q]\) survives. Thus
\[[c]\mapsto[r+q]\mapsto[q].\]
The Week 4 notes show the complete matrices and induced maps.

title: Week 4: Persistent homology
text:
Software changes the scale notation
Week 3 used ball radius \(r\): \(d(x_i,x_j)\leq2r\).
ripser reports the distance threshold
\[\varepsilon=2r.\]
Name the convention before interpreting coordinates.

title: Week 4: Persistent homology
text:
Persistence is not importance
Long interval means survival across the selected filtration range.
It does not automatically mean scientific relevance, statistical surprise, predictive value or robustness to a different model.

title: Week 4: Persistent homology
text:
Perturb, recompute, compare
The walkthrough now computes a persistence diagram, slightly perturbs the observations and computes a second diagram.
We need to ask:

Which points correspond?
How large is the worst movement after the best matching?
Can a small input change cause an arbitrarily large output change?

The first two questions motivate bottleneck distance. The third motivates the stability theorem.

title: Week 4: Persistent homology
text:
Bottleneck distance
Match diagram points to each other or to the diagonal.
\[d_B(D,E)=\text{smallest possible worst matching cost}.\]
Deleting a bar \([b,d)\) by matching it to the diagonal costs
\[\frac{d-b}{2}.\]

title: Week 4: Persistent homology
text:
A stability theorem
Fix a homology dimension and coefficient field.
For tame \(f,g:X\to\mathbb R\) on the same triangulable space, using sublevel sets:
\[
d_B(D_p(f),D_p(g))
\leq
\|f-g\|_\infty.
\]
If \(|f(x)-g(x)|\leq\delta\) everywhere, their diagrams differ by at most \(\delta\) in bottleneck distance.
Here tame means that only finitely many homological changes occur in the filtration.
Triangulable means that \(X\) has the topological type of a simplicial complex. It is a classical regularity hypothesis that excludes pathological spaces and makes the homology changes manageable. Later formulations use broader tameness conditions.

title: Week 4: Persistent homology
text:
What the bound means
After the best matching, allowing matches to the diagonal:

every birth-death point moves by at most \(\delta\);
a bar longer than \(2\delta\) cannot simply be matched away; and
small uniform function noise cannot cause an arbitrarily large diagram change.

† Qualification. Different point clouds, metrics or filtrations require their own stability result and input distance.
Stability controls sensitivity, not scientific meaning.

title: Week 4: Persistent homology
text:
◷ Why stability mattered historically
2002: persistence and its algorithm.
2005: the algebraic and barcode framework.
2007: stability supplied the robustness guarantee needed for noisy data.

controlled input perturbation \(\Longrightarrow\) controlled diagram perturbation

It made persistence compelling for data analysis, but it does not validate the modelling choices before the theorem is applied.

title: Week 4: Persistent homology
text:
Applied translation
Birth: a new independent organisation becomes detectable.
Death: it merges or becomes filled under the construction.
Persistence: the range over which it stays distinguishable.
Then ask: under which representation, metric and filtration?

title: Week 4: Persistent homology
text:
Before we leave

Which maps carry cross-scale information?
Which assumptions justify the barcode?
Which scale convention did the software report?
What baseline must the feature beat?

See the applied glossary for the running translation layer.

3. Implement: participant checkpoint

A. Point cloud: Rips filtration
GUDHI uses the pairwise-distance threshold as the Rips filtration value. Construct only through dimension 2 because that is enough to calculate \(H_1\).

st_point.compute_persistence(homology_coeff_field=2)
D1_point=finite_intervals(st_point,1)
print('simplices:',st_point.num_simplices(),'longest finite H1:',round(longest(D1_point),3))




B. Weighted graph: graph or clique complex?
Keep vertices and edge weights fixed. First retain only the graph, then expand every clique through dimension 2.
Checkpoint. Predict which version can fill the cycle on vertices \(0,1,2\). After running, check that both versions contain the same six edges before comparing \(H_1\).


Code
def weighted_graph_tree(fill_cliques):
    st = gd.SimplexTree()
    for vertex in range(5):
        st.insert([vertex], filtration=0.0)
    for edge, weight in graph_edges.items():
        st.insert(edge, filtration=weight)
    if fill_cliques:
        st.expansion(2)
    st.make_filtration_non_decreasing()
    st.compute_persistence(homology_coeff_field=2, persistence_dim_max=True)
    return st

# TODO: change only this switch, then compare the two stored results.
versions = {'graph only': False, 'clique complex': True}
graph_results = {}
for name, fill_cliques in versions.items():
    tree = weighted_graph_tree(fill_cliques)
    graph_results[name] = tree
    print(name, 'simplices:', tree.num_simplices(),
          'H1:', tree.persistence_intervals_in_dimension(1))




C. Scalar field: cubical sublevel filtration
The top-dimensional cells carry field values and low values enter first. In two dimensions, each array entry is treated as a filled square 2-cell. Its boundary edges and corner vertices are included with it. The persistence coordinates are therefore field values, not distances.

title: Week 5: Static data in practice
text:
Computational cautions
Rips complexes grow quickly. For an \(N\)-point cloud, the Vietoris–Rips filtration contains \(O(N^2)\) edges, \(O(N^3)\) triangles, \(O(N^4)\) tetrahedra and so on. Even when truncating at dimension 2, the size can scale like \(O(N^3)\). This is why the choice of maximum dimension, maximum filtration value and sparsification strategy is not merely technical.
More precisely, a Rips complex can contain as many as \(\binom{N}{k+1}\) simplices in dimension \(k\). Homology in dimension \(p\) depends on two boundary maps,
\[
C_{p+1}\xrightarrow{\partial_{p+1}}C_p
\xrightarrow{\partial_p}C_{p-1},
\]
so the complex must normally be constructed through dimension \(p+1\):









Homology requested
Structures being detected
Highest simplices needed to decide whether they are filled
Worst-case count of those simplices




\(H_0\)
connected components
edges
\(\binom N2\)


\(H_1\)
edge cycles or loops
triangles
\(\binom N3\)


\(H_2\)
closed triangular surfaces or cavities
tetrahedra
\(\binom N4\)


\(H_p\)
\(p\)-cycles
\((p+1)\)-simplices
\(\binom N{p+2}\)



This is the central dimensional cost. Moving from \(H_1\) to \(H_2\) does not merely add another row to the output: it can replace a triangle-scale construction with a tetrahedron-scale one. The boundary matrix \([\partial_{p+1}]\) has one column for every \((p+1)\)-simplex and one row for every \(p\)-simplex. Storing and reducing that matrix can dominate both memory and runtime even when the final barcode contains only a few intervals.

▶ Likely sticking point. Setting max_dimension=1 is not generally enough to compute correct \(H_1\). It retains the graph cycles but omits triangles, the 2-simplices that can make those cycles boundaries. An omitted triangle can turn a class that should die into an apparently essential class. Conversely, constructing dimensions above \(p+1\) cannot change \(H_p\) and wastes resources.

The ambient coordinate dimension and homological dimension are different. A point cloud in \(\mathbb R^{20}\) may still be analysed only in \(H_0\) and \(H_1\); requesting \(H_{20}\) is neither automatic nor usually feasible. Report the largest homology degree requested, the largest simplex dimension constructed and the reason for both.

section: One implementation pattern, three data types
text:
One implementation pattern, three data types






TipCompare the three workflows



The lecture walkthrough narrates how a point cloud, weighted graph and scalar grid become different filtered objects. The participant practical lets you vary one modelling choice in each workflow and explain whether the scientific question has changed.


The Week 5 notebooks use GUDHI throughout. A Rips complex represents a metric point cloud, a simplex tree stores a weighted graph and optionally expands its cliques, and a cubical complex represents a gridded field. Using one stack makes the object changes easier to see. It does not imply that one library or complex is best for every application.
A lower-star filtration begins with values on vertices and assigns a simplex the maximum value of its vertices. In the cubical practical, GUDHI instead receives values on top-dimensional grid cells: pixels in two dimensions or voxels in three. Each pixel is treated as a filled square 2-cell, not merely as a plotted dot. When a square enters, its four boundary edges and four corner vertices are included automatically.

Worked example: read a cubical sublevel filtration



A cubical sublevel filtration on a scalar grid.


The filtration contains every cell whose value is at most \(a\):

at \(a=1\), the value-1 pixels form a ring and an \(H_1\) class is present;
at \(a=4\), more squares enter but the value-5 centre is still absent, so the opening remains; and
at \(a=5\), the central square enters and fills the opening, so the class dies.

The birth and death coordinates are therefore scalar-field values. They are not Euclidean distances. Negating the field would reveal high-valued regions first, changing the scientific question rather than merely changing a software setting.

title: Week 5: Static data in practice
text:
Implementation clinics






NoteChoose one clinic first



The three clinics are alternative routes for different data types, not three new theories to master in one sitting. Work through the clinic closest to your data in full. Use the other two to compare how the observed object changes the appropriate representation.



Implementation clinic 1: state cloud
Starting object. Seventy sampled states form a noisy annular point cloud.
Choice. Use Euclidean distance and a Rips pairwise threshold, construct through dimension 2 to compute \(H_1\), and stop at threshold 1.8.
Prediction. Short edges connect neighbouring samples into a loop. At a larger threshold, Rips triangles should eventually fill it.
Software audit. Record the 70 observations, total simplex count, maximum simplex dimension, coefficient field and the fact that GUDHI’s parameter is a pairwise-distance threshold rather than a ball radius.
Controlled comparison. Retain every other observation and repeat the same pipeline. This tests sampling sensitivity while holding representation, metric and construction fixed. It does not test a different notion of closeness.


Implementation clinic 2: weighted interaction graph
Starting object. Five vertices have weighted edges
\[
01:0.30,\quad12:0.40,\quad02:0.45,
\quad23:0.70,\quad34:0.80,\quad24:0.85.
\]
The filtration contains all edges with weight at most \(a\).
Graph-only prediction. At \(a=0.45\), edge \(02\) closes the cycle \(0\!-!1\!-!2\!-!0\). At \(a=0.85\), edge \(24\) closes the second cycle \(2\!-!3\!-!4\!-!2\). With no 2-simplices available, both graph cycles remain unfilled. GUDHI reports \(H_1\) intervals \([0.45,\infty)\) and \([0.85,\infty)\).
Clique-complex prediction. Expanding cliques adds triangle \([0,1,2]\) at 0.45 and triangle \([2,3,4]\) at 0.85. Each face enters at the same value as its last edge and immediately makes the corresponding edge cycle a boundary. There are therefore no positive-length \(H_1\) intervals.
Choice exposed. The vertices, weighted edges and thresholds did not change. Only the assertion “every three-clique is a filled 2-simplex” changed. This is a representation comparison, not numerical robustness testing.


Implementation clinic 3: scalar field
Starting object. On a \(45\times45\) grid, the notebook evaluates
\[
f(x,y)=\bigl(x^2+y^2-1\bigr)^2.
\]
Values are smallest near the unit circle, equal to 1 at the origin and larger far from the circle.
Construction. Treat every array entry as a filled square carrying its field value and use a cubical sublevel filtration. Low-valued squares near the unit circle enter first.
Prediction. The early squares form an annular band, creating an \(H_1\) class. The centre remains absent until the threshold approaches \(f(0,0)=1\), when it fills the opening.
Computed check. At this grid resolution, the main interval is approximately \([0.0055,1.0000)\). The small nonzero birth reflects the fact that the discrete grid does not sample the unit circle exactly. Its death agrees with the central field value.
Choice exposed. Repeating the calculation on \(-f\) includes the original high-valued regions first. That is a superlevel analysis of \(f\) and answers a different question; it is not a harmless sign convention or sensitivity check.

text:
This is the live worked example, built around a synthetic ring that fills in and re-forms. It follows the conceptual argument of the slides through prediction, reveal and interpretation. It is not intended as a line-by-line answer key to the participant practical.
Resource boundary. The reference notes distinguish representation time, physical time and filtration scale. The slides stage that distinction visually. This notebook completes the framewise calculation and CROCKER-style summary. The participant practical leaves a representation choice and the interpretation boundary to students.
Lecture map. Build the state-space representation, inspect selected frames, predict the time course of loop evidence, and then reveal the two-axis summary. End by asking what feature identity would require beyond repeated persistence.
We compute ordinary Rips persistence independently at each frame of a synthetic evolving point cloud. The output is a time series of diagrams and a CROCKER-style rank surface. No feature identity is asserted across frames.
Presenter route. Use the ring-to-disk-to-ring sequence to keep physical time separate from filtration scale and to show why repeated diagrams do not track identity.
Code
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
RNG=np.random.default_rng(3024)
from ripser import ripser

def betti_curve(D,grid): return np.array([np.sum((D[:,0]<=a)&(a<D[:,1])) for a in grid])
def max_persistence(D):
 F=D[np.isfinite(D[:,1])]; return float(np.max(F[:,1]-F[:,0])) if len(F) else 0.

title: Week 7 lecture walkthrough: repeated persistence through physical time
text:
Representation bridge: delay coordinates
A scalar signal is not yet a state-space point cloud. For lag \(\tau\) and dimension \(m\) construct
\[\Phi_{m,\tau}(t)=\bigl(x(t),x(t-\tau),\ldots,x(t-(m-1)\tau)\bigr).\]
The code below uses index lag rather than physical units. Predict the shape for a periodic signal. Then change only lag and describe what geometric organisation changes. Temporal order is not retained by the later Rips calculation unless it is stored separately.


Code
def delay_coordinates(signal, dimension, lag):
    rows = len(signal) - (dimension - 1) * lag
    return np.column_stack([
        signal[(dimension - 1 - j) * lag:(dimension - 1 - j) * lag + rows]
        for j in range(dimension)
    ])

sample_times = np.linspace(0, 8 * np.pi, 500)
signal = np.sin(sample_times)
lag = 25
embedded = delay_coordinates(signal, dimension=2, lag=lag)
plt.figure(figsize=(4, 4))
plt.plot(embedded[:, 0], embedded[:, 1], linewidth=1)
plt.gca().set_aspect('equal')
plt.xlabel(r'$x(t)$'); plt.ylabel(r'$x(t-\tau)$')
plt.show()
print('embedded shape:', embedded.shape, 'index lag:', lag)

title: Week 7 lecture walkthrough: repeated persistence through physical time
section: Expert optional subtopic: a SW1PerS-style periodicity score
text:
Expert optional subtopic: a SW1PerS-style periodicity score
Sliding-window persistence turns recurrence of signal phase into loop evidence. Compare a sinusoid with a chirp after centring and normalising every window. This demonstrates the SW1PerS intuition without claiming to reproduce every calibration step in the published algorithm.


Code
def forward_windows(signal, dimension, lag):
    rows = len(signal) - dimension * lag
    W = np.column_stack([signal[j*lag:j*lag+rows] for j in range(dimension+1)])
    W = W - W.mean(axis=1, keepdims=True)
    return W / np.maximum(np.linalg.norm(W, axis=1, keepdims=True), 1e-12)

u = np.linspace(0, 12*np.pi, 900)
signals = {'periodic': np.sin(u), 'chirp': np.sin(u + 0.018*u**2)}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 3.5))
for ax, (name, values) in zip(axes, signals.items()):
    W = forward_windows(values, dimension=8, lag=8)[::4]
    diagram = ripser(W, maxdim=1)['dgms'][1]
    ax.scatter(W[:,0], W[:,1], s=8, alpha=.65)
    ax.set_title(f'{name}: max H1 = {max_persistence(diagram):.3f}')
    ax.set_aspect('equal')
plt.show()

title: Week 7 lecture walkthrough: repeated persistence through physical time
section: Expert optional subtopic: scale by codensity
text:
Expert optional subtopic: scale by codensity
A plot with time and scale is not automatically a multiparameter module. Here both directions really do give inclusions. Codensity is distance to the fifth nearest neighbour. Raising \(\delta\) admits less densely sampled points; raising \(\varepsilon\) adds Rips simplices. We display \(\beta_1(\delta,\varepsilon)\), a dimension-function summary rather than a complete multiparameter barcode.


Code
angles = RNG.uniform(0, 2*np.pi, 90)
cloud = np.c_[np.cos(angles), np.sin(angles)] + 0.045*RNG.normal(size=(90,2))
cloud = np.vstack([cloud, RNG.uniform(-1.3, 1.3, size=(25,2))])
pairwise = np.linalg.norm(cloud[:,None,:] - cloud[None,:,:], axis=2)
codensity = np.sort(pairwise, axis=1)[:,5]
delta_grid = np.quantile(codensity, [0.35, 0.55, 0.75, 1.0])
epsilon_grid = np.linspace(0, 1.0, 80)
rows = []
for delta in delta_grid:
    retained = cloud[codensity <= delta]
    diagram = ripser(retained, maxdim=1)['dgms'][1]
    rows.append(betti_curve(diagram, epsilon_grid))
bifiltration_summary = np.vstack(rows)
plt.figure(figsize=(7,3.5))
plt.imshow(bifiltration_summary, origin='lower', aspect='auto',
           extent=[epsilon_grid[0], epsilon_grid[-1], 0, len(delta_grid)-1])
plt.yticks(range(len(delta_grid)), [f'{d:.2f}' for d in delta_grid])
plt.xlabel('Rips scale ε'); plt.ylabel('codensity threshold δ')
plt.colorbar(label='β1'); plt.title('Scale-by-codensity dimension function')
plt.show()
print('grid shape:', bifiltration_summary.shape)

Week 7 distinguishes three constructions: repeated persistence through physical time, sliding-window persistence for periodicity, and a genuine two-parameter bifiltration.

title: Week 7: Time varying data, periodicity and multiparameter persistence
text:
Mathematics and summaries
This is not genuinely dynamic topology in the strongest sense because no method has identified a specific feature across time. It is repeated static persistence.
◇ Object check. At each time \(t\), there may be a complete ordinary persistence module \(V_t\) and its diagram \(D_t\). What is absent is a coherent family of maps connecting \(V_s\) to \(V_t\). A time series of diagrams is therefore not yet a vineyard module.

title: Week 7: Time varying data, periodicity and multiparameter persistence
section: A scalar time series is not yet a point cloud
text:
A scalar time series is not yet a point cloud
\[\Phi_{m,\tau}(t)=\bigl(x(t),x(t-\tau),\ldots,x(t-(m-1)\tau)\bigr).\]
Choose lag, dimension, sampling and window length.
Point-cloud persistence does not retain temporal order by itself.

title: Week 7: Time varying data, periodicity and multiparameter persistence
text:
Two axes, two meanings
Physical time \(t\): when the system is observed.
Filtration scale \(\varepsilon\): threshold inside one static computation.
\[C_p(t,\varepsilon)=\#\{(b,d)\in D_t^{(p)}:b\leq\varepsilon<d\}.\]

title: Week 7: Time varying data, periodicity and multiparameter persistence
text:
What a CROCKER-style plot says
CROCKER: Contour Realization Of Computed \(k\)-dimensional hole Evolution in the Rips complex.
It displays \(\beta_k(t,\varepsilon)\) through time and scale.
It can reveal transitions and regimes.
It forgets birth-death pairing and does not identify a class across frames.

title: Week 7: Time varying data, periodicity and multiparameter persistence
text:
SW1PerS: periodicity as a loop
\[\operatorname{SW}_{m,\tau}x(t)
=(x(t),x(t+\tau),\ldots,x(t+m\tau)).\]
A periodic signal repeatedly visits the same phases, producing a loop-like sliding-window cloud after centring and normalising.
Persistent \(H_1\) measures the strength of that loop. Lag, window length and sampling remain modelling choices.

title: Week 7: Time varying data, periodicity and multiparameter persistence
section: Two axes do not automatically make a bifiltration
text:
Two axes do not automatically make a bifiltration
Independent frames \(X_t\) need not satisfy \(X_t\subseteq X_{t+1}\).
For codensity \(q(x)\), instead let
\[X_\delta=\{x:q(x)\leq\delta\},\qquad
K_{\delta,\varepsilon}=\operatorname{VR}_\varepsilon(X_\delta).\]
Increasing either \(\delta\) or \(\varepsilon\) gives inclusions: this is a genuine two-parameter module.

title: Week 7: Time varying data, periodicity and multiparameter persistence
text:
Window length is modelling
Short: poor sampling. Long: mixed regimes. Overlap: smoother but more dependent.

title: Week 7: Repeated persistence through time
Week 7: Repeated persistence through time
text:
Mathematics and summaries

What is the object at each time?
Several kinds of observations can be repeated through time. The notation is a compact menu, not a list of objects that was previously defined as one family:








Symbol
Object available at time \(t\)
Typical source




\(X_t\)
metric point cloud
agent positions or a window of state vectors


\(G_t\)
graph
a changing interaction or contact network


\(I_t\)
image or gridded scalar field
density, activity or spatial concentration


\(W_t\)
sliding-window point cloud
delay vectors made from a signal near time \(t\)


\(K_{\bullet,t}\)
a complete filtration at fixed \(t\)
complexes \(K_{\varepsilon,t}\) across scale \(\varepsilon\)



For example, a moving swarm supplies point clouds \(X_t\). Choosing a Rips construction at each frame produces \(K_{\varepsilon,t}\), and homology produces a diagram \(D_t\). The complete chain is
\[
\text{observation at }t
\longrightarrow K_{\varepsilon,t}
\longrightarrow H_p(K_{\varepsilon,t})
\longrightarrow D_t.
\]
The same notation does not imply that \(X_t\subseteq X_{t+1}\) or that a map between consecutive frames exists.


From a time series to a state-space cloud






TipKeep the two notions of time visible



The lecture walkthrough follows a time series through delay coordinates, framewise persistence and a CROCKER-style display. The participant practical asks you to vary a representation choice while keeping physical time distinct from filtration scale.


For a scalar observation \(x(t)\), a delay-coordinate representation is
\[
\Phi_{m,\tau}(t)=
\bigl(x(t),x(t-\tau),\ldots,x(t-(m-1)\tau)\bigr).
\]
The lag \(\tau\), embedding dimension \(m\), sampling interval and window length are upstream modelling choices. Treating the resulting vectors as a point cloud usually discards their temporal ordering unless time is retained separately. Sampling speed also changes point density: slow passage through a region can create many nearby points without creating a new invariant set.
For multivariate observations, the measured state vector may already be a usable representation, but coordinate scaling, periodic variables and unobserved state still require attention.



A scalar signal is converted to a delay-coordinate cloud; repeating persistence in windows produces a summary indexed by physical time and filtration scale.


This is not genuinely dynamic topology in the strongest sense because no method has identified a specific feature across time. It is repeated static persistence.
◇ Object check. At each time \(t\), there may be a complete ordinary persistence module \(V_t\) and its diagram \(D_t\). What is absent is a coherent family of maps connecting \(V_s\) to \(V_t\). A time series of diagrams is therefore not yet a vineyard module.
Useful outputs include

framewise diagrams;
sliding-window diagrams;
Betti curves through scale;
Betti summaries through physical time;
diagram distances to a baseline;
CROCKER-style plots, which project repeated persistence into a rank-function-like summary across scale and time.

Writing \(D_t\) for the diagram at physical time \(t\), a CROCKER-style surface records
\[
C_p(t,\varepsilon)=\#\{(b,d)\in D_t^{(p)}:b\leq\varepsilon<d\}.
\]
This is the framewise Betti number across a two-dimensional display. It can reveal regimes and transitions, but it does not connect a class at time \(s\) to a class at time \(t\).
CROCKER stands for Contour Realization Of Computed \(k\)-dimensional hole Evolution in the Rips complex. The construction was introduced by Topaz, Ziegelmeier and Halverson for biological aggregation models (Topaz et al. 2015). One vertical slice is the Betti curve of one frame; one horizontal slice shows how the number of features alive at a chosen scale changes with physical time. A contour or heat map makes regimes visible, but forgets birth-death pairing and feature identity. CROCKER stacks add a persistence threshold so that short bars can be suppressed (Xian et al. 2022).
Window length is part of the observation model. Short windows may be undersampled; long windows can mix regimes and turn temporal change into apparent spatial structure.

A topological summary can change through time without any individual hole being tracked through time.

title: Week 7: Repeated persistence through time
text:
Optional subtopics
The following routes use persistence for related but different questions. Their high-level ideas are useful; their detailed development can be skipped unless they match the participant’s data.

SW1PerS and periodicity
Sliding-window coordinates turn a scalar signal into a point cloud. A persistent loop can quantify repeated traversal of one periodic phase cycle. This is a periodicity method, not a way to track a class across changing frames.


Multiparameter persistence
A genuine bifiltration retains two jointly ordered construction parameters. It requires compatible inclusions in both directions; merely plotting physical time against filtration scale is not enough.

title: Week 7: Repeated persistence through time
text:
What Week 7 adds
The core method describes how static topological summaries change through physical time. It is often the honest first dynamic analysis. The optional subtopics answer different questions and should be selected only when their additional structure is scientifically needed.

title: Sources and data provenance

Candidate public datasets
These are development candidates, not bundled course data. Before adopting one, retain its licence and provenance, create a documented teaching subset, and state the preprocessing and interpretation limits.

Fish-school collective U-turn trajectories
The Dryad collection is the strongest match to the dynamical and complex systems audience. One short trial could support point-cloud or interaction-graph constructions, repeated persistence and a later zigzag discussion. Compare any topology with speed, polarisation, nearest-neighbour distance and recorded U-turn times. The full collection is large, so a teaching version should use one small, documented trial.


MIT-BIH Arrhythmia Database
The PhysioNet collection could support delay-coordinate clouds from short ECG windows and comparisons through annotated rhythm transitions. Compare with heart rate, spectral power and beat annotations, and vary delay, embedding dimension and window length. Use only short, non-diagnostic excerpts and make no clinical claim.


NASA IMS bearing degradation data
The bearing dataset offers an industry route through vibration windows over a run-to-failure experiment. Compare persistence summaries with RMS vibration, kurtosis and spectral features. A course version should provide a small pre-indexed subset rather than the full raw archive.


UCI Human Activity Recognition
The smartphone activity dataset could compare accelerometer and gyroscope windows across activities or through postural transitions. Compare with covariance, spectral and classification baselines. Subject-level splitting is essential because overlapping windows must not be treated as independent observations.


UCI Air Quality
The air-quality sensor dataset could support multivariate state clouds, sensor drift and later two-parameter questions. Compare with PCA, regression residuals and seasonality. Missing values encoded as \(-200\) must be removed before computing distances, and the reuse terms should be resolved before redistributing a derived course file.

title: Topological Data Analysis for Static and Dynamic Data
text:
This MasterClass develops the judgement needed to read, compute, question and adapt persistent homology pipelines for static and dynamic data.
The central outcome is conceptual fluency. By the end of the course, you should be able to follow the mathematical argument in a technical TDA paper, identify the objects and maps being used, and judge what its conclusions do and do not say about the underlying system. We construct examples and run computations because doing so makes the ideas inspectable, not because implementing every method from scratch is the final goal.
It is not organised as a software tutorial. The recurring question is:

title: Topological Data Analysis for Static and Dynamic Data
text:
The guiding construction for Weeks 1–4
The expression below is likely to look like another language at first. It is included now because it is the destination of the first four weeks, not because you are expected to understand it already. Each week makes a different part of it readable.
Given a filtration of simplicial complexes
\[
K_a\subseteq K_b\qquad\text{whenever }a\leq b,
\]
its \(p\)-dimensional persistent homology over a field \(\mathbb F\) is the persistence module
\[
a\longmapsto H_p(K_a;\mathbb F),
\qquad
(a\leq b)\longmapsto
(\iota_{a,b})_*:H_p(K_a;\mathbb F)\to H_p(K_b;\mathbb F).
\]
This says more than “compute holes at several scales”. It retains the homology vector space at every scale and the maps recording what each earlier class becomes later. Under suitable one-parameter finiteness or tameness conditions, the module decomposes into interval modules and can be summarised by a barcode or persistence diagram. The barcode is therefore a representation of the persistence module, not the starting definition.

How to read the formula aloud

At every parameter value \(a\), build a representation \(K_a\) of the data and compute its \(p\)-dimensional homology. Whenever \(a\leq b\), the smaller representation sits inside the larger one, and this inclusion tells us what every homology class at \(a\) becomes at \(b\). Persistent homology is the whole linked family of homology spaces and maps.

The data are not explicitly visible in the displayed definition. They enter earlier, when observations are turned into the family of representations \(K_a\). That step contains modelling choices: what is observed, how it is preprocessed, what distance or relation is used, what construction produces \(K_a\), and what parameter \(a\) controls. The formula begins after those choices have been made. Further choices remain visible in the homological dimension \(p\) and coefficient field \(\mathbb F\).
Here is how the four weeks make the expression readable:

Week 1: scientific object, observations and representation. Why might connectedness, recurrence or enclosure be worth preserving, and what information is deliberately forgotten by a topological lens?
Week 2: \(K_a\) and \(H_p(K_a;\mathbb F)\). What is a simplicial complex, how do boundary maps define homology, and what does the coefficient field change?
Week 3: the nested family \(K_a\subseteq K_b\). How does a metric, relation or filtration function produce complexes that grow with a parameter?
Week 4: the maps \((\iota_{a,b})_*\) and their interval summary. How do homology classes persist, merge or become boundaries, and when may the resulting module be represented by a barcode?







ImportantRunning the code



Website code boxes are static previews. Download the participant .ipynb file from each weekly page and run it directly in JupyterLab, Jupyter Notebook or VS Code. You do not need to copy individual cells.
Set up the environment and run a practical

The participant practical is the student-facing notebook used during independent work. The lecture walkthrough is an instructor resource used to control prediction and reveal during the lecture. It can be released to students after the session as a worked record, but it is not intended to remove the decisions from the practical in advance.

title: Topological Data Analysis for Static and Dynamic Data
text:
Who this course is for


Dynamical systems researchers
Use topology alongside geometric, temporal and statistical descriptions of trajectories, attractors and collective dynamics.


Honours and graduate students
Build the algebraic topology foundations needed to understand what TDA software constructs and computes.


Applied and industry participants
Evaluate whether connectedness, loops or multiscale organisation answer an operational question beyond existing baselines.


No prior algebraic topology is assumed. Topology refresher A begins with the familiar coffee-cup and doughnut intuition; Topology refresher B keeps formal open-set and continuity details available without making them prerequisites. Familiarity with basic linear algebra is helpful; the pre-Week 2 algebra survival guide supplies a concise refresher at the point where it is needed. The practical notebooks introduce the required Python code as it is used.

title: Topological Data Analysis for Static and Dynamic Data
text:
Software scope
Python is the course’s primary computing environment because it gives participants a coherent route through point-cloud, simplicial, cubical and persistence workflows. The notebooks use focused, inspectable code before calling specialist packages such as Ripser.py or GUDHI. The notebook setup page explains how to run them.
Julia is a planned research extension, especially when the surrounding dynamical simulation is already Julia-native or a Ripserer.jl benchmark is scientifically useful. It is not introduced merely to reproduce the same classroom barcode in a second language. A mixed-language project should pass simple objects—point arrays, distance matrices or persistence intervals—across the Python/Julia boundary rather than live complex objects. Zigzag, multiparameter and vineyard-module computation require separate method and software evaluation; ordinary persistence software does not provide them automatically.

title: Topological Data Analysis for Static and Dynamic Data
section: Guiding texts and how the course uses them
text:
Guiding texts and how the course uses them
Two books support the first half of the course, but they play different roles.
Edelsbrunner and Harer, Computational Topology provides the main mathematical and computational spine (Edelsbrunner and Harer 2010). We draw on its movement between geometry, topology and algorithms: connectedness in Chapter I.1; simplicial complexes, nerves, Delaunay complexes and alpha complexes in Chapter III; homology and matrix reduction in Chapter IV; one-parameter persistence and its reduction algorithm in Chapter VII; and vineyards, diagram distances and stability in Chapter VIII. It is especially useful when the course asks how a topological construction becomes something that can be represented and computed.
Postol, Algebraic Topology for Data Scientists provides the more gradual preparatory and data-facing route (Postol 2024). We use Chapter 2 for sets, metrics, topological spaces, continuity and connectedness; Chapter 3 for fields, vector spaces and the algebraic vocabulary behind homology; Chapter 4.1 for simplicial homology and induced maps; and selected parts of Chapter 5 for Rips complexes, persistence modules, barcodes, diagram distances, sublevel sets, graphs, time series, persistence images and zigzag persistence. The course does not rely on the book’s later specialised chapters on cohomology, homotopy, obstruction theory or cohomology operations.
Neither book determines the applications or software workflow. Weeks 5–8 use research papers and software documentation attached directly to the relevant week. All readings are optional routes for checking a definition, seeing a second explanation or following an idea into the literature.

title: Week 7 lecture walkthrough: repeated persistence through physical time
text:
This is the live worked example, built around a synthetic ring that fills in and re-forms. It follows the conceptual argument of the slides through prediction, reveal and interpretation. It is not intended as a line-by-line answer key to the participant practical.
Resource boundary. The reference notes distinguish representation time, physical time and filtration scale. The slides stage that distinction visually. This notebook completes the framewise calculation and CROCKER-style summary. The participant practical leaves a representation choice and the interpretation boundary to students.
Lecture map. Build the state-space representation, inspect selected frames, predict the time course of loop evidence, and then reveal the two-axis summary. End by asking what feature identity would require beyond repeated persistence.
We compute ordinary Rips persistence independently at each frame of a synthetic evolving point cloud. The output is a time series of diagrams and a CROCKER-style rank surface. No feature identity is asserted across frames.
Presenter route. Use the ring-to-disk-to-ring sequence to keep physical time separate from filtration scale and to show why repeated diagrams do not track identity.
Code
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
RNG=np.random.default_rng(3024)
from ripser import ripser

def betti_curve(D,grid): return np.array([np.sum((D[:,0]<=a)&(a<D[:,1])) for a in grid])
def max_persistence(D):
 F=D[np.isfinite(D[:,1])]; return float(np.max(F[:,1]-F[:,0])) if len(F) else 0.

title: Week 7 lecture walkthrough: repeated persistence through physical time
text:
Representation bridge: delay coordinates
A scalar signal is not yet a state-space point cloud. For lag \(\tau\) and dimension \(m\) construct
\[\Phi_{m,\tau}(t)=\bigl(x(t),x(t-\tau),\ldots,x(t-(m-1)\tau)\bigr).\]
The code below uses index lag rather than physical units. Predict the shape for a periodic signal. Then change only lag and describe what geometric organisation changes. Temporal order is not retained by the later Rips calculation unless it is stored separately.


Code
def delay_coordinates(signal, dimension, lag):
    rows = len(signal) - (dimension - 1) * lag
    return np.column_stack([
        signal[(dimension - 1 - j) * lag:(dimension - 1 - j) * lag + rows]
        for j in range(dimension)
    ])

sample_times = np.linspace(0, 8 * np.pi, 500)
signal = np.sin(sample_times)
lag = 25
embedded = delay_coordinates(signal, dimension=2, lag=lag)
plt.figure(figsize=(4, 4))
plt.plot(embedded[:, 0], embedded[:, 1], linewidth=1)
plt.gca().set_aspect('equal')
plt.xlabel(r'$x(t)$'); plt.ylabel(r'$x(t-\tau)$')
plt.show()
print('embedded shape:', embedded.shape, 'index lag:', lag)

title: Week 7 lecture walkthrough: repeated persistence through physical time
text:

Presenter cue. Show the object before the calculation. Ask the room to separate what is given from what will be constructed.
The synthetic system moves from a coherent ring to a filled cloud and back. The samples at each frame are observations of a changing representation. The point labels are reused only to generate smooth motion; persistence does not use those labels.

Construct a CROCKER-style surface \(\beta_1(t,\varepsilon)\): each cell counts intervals alive at physical time \(t\) and Rips threshold \(\varepsilon\). Compare it with the simpler radial coefficient-of-variation baseline.

5. Interpret: lecture demonstration
Presenter close. Ask what the example supports, what information was discarded and which stronger claim would be unjustified.

Which axis is physical time and which is filtration scale?
What statement can the rank surface support without feature tracking?
When would a sliding window blur a transition or create apparent persistence?
Does topology add information beyond radial variation in this synthetic example?
What extra maps or correspondences would be required to claim feature identity?

† Qualification. A smooth time series of summaries is still repeated static persistence. It is not a vineyard or vineyard module.
The rank surface supports statements about how the distribution of topological lifetimes changes with time and scale. It does not label a class across frames. In this designed ring-to-disk example, radial variation is already a strong baseline, so the demonstration motivates method comparison rather than superiority.

Return to the final slide questions.

title: Week 7 lecture walkthrough: repeated persistence through physical time
section: Expert optional subtopic: a SW1PerS-style periodicity score
text:
Expert optional subtopic: a SW1PerS-style periodicity score
Sliding-window persistence turns recurrence of signal phase into loop evidence. Compare a sinusoid with a chirp after centring and normalising every window. This demonstrates the SW1PerS intuition without claiming to reproduce every calibration step in the published algorithm.


Code
def forward_windows(signal, dimension, lag):
    rows = len(signal) - dimension * lag
    W = np.column_stack([signal[j*lag:j*lag+rows] for j in range(dimension+1)])
    W = W - W.mean(axis=1, keepdims=True)
    return W / np.maximum(np.linalg.norm(W, axis=1, keepdims=True), 1e-12)

u = np.linspace(0, 12*np.pi, 900)
signals = {'periodic': np.sin(u), 'chirp': np.sin(u + 0.018*u**2)}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 3.5))
for ax, (name, values) in zip(axes, signals.items()):

text:
Expert optional subtopic: scale by codensity
A plot with time and scale is not automatically a multiparameter module. Here both directions really do give inclusions. Codensity is distance to the fifth nearest neighbour. Raising \(\delta\) admits less densely sampled points; raising \(\varepsilon\) adds Rips simplices. We display \(\beta_1(\delta,\varepsilon)\), a dimension-function summary rather than a complete multiparameter barcode.


Code
angles = RNG.uniform(0, 2*np.pi, 90)
cloud = np.c_[np.cos(angles), np.sin(angles)] + 0.045*RNG.normal(size=(90,2))
cloud = np.vstack([cloud, RNG.uniform(-1.3, 1.3, size=(25,2))])
pairwise = np.linalg.norm(cloud[:,None,:] - cloud[None,:,:], axis=2)
codensity = np.sort(pairwise, axis=1)[:,5]
delta_grid = np.quantile(codensity, [0.35, 0.55, 0.75, 1.0])
epsilon_grid = np.linspace(0, 1.0, 80)
rows = []
for delta in delta_grid:
    retained = cloud[codensity <= delta]
    diagram = ripser(retained, maxdim=1)['dgms'][1]
    rows.append(betti_curve(diagram, epsilon_grid))
bifiltration_summary = np.vstack(rows)
plt.figure(figsize=(7,3.5))
plt.imshow(bifiltration_summary, origin='lower', aspect='auto',
           extent=[epsilon_grid[0], epsilon_grid[-1], 0, len(delta_grid)-1])
plt.yticks(range(len(delta_grid)), [f'{d:.2f}' for d in delta_grid])
plt.xlabel('Rips scale ε'); plt.ylabel('codensity threshold δ')
plt.colorbar(label='β1'); plt.title('Scale-by-codensity dimension function')
plt.show()
print('grid shape:', bifiltration_summary.shape)

Representation bridge: delay coordinates
A scalar signal is not yet a state-space point cloud. For lag \(\tau\) and dimension \(m\) construct
\[\Phi_{m,\tau}(t)=\bigl(x(t),x(t-\tau),\ldots,x(t-(m-1)\tau)\bigr).\]
The code below uses index lag rather than physical units. Predict the shape for a periodic signal. Then change only lag and describe what geometric organisation changes. Temporal order is not retained by the later Rips calculation unless it is stored separately.

def delay_coordinates(signal, dimension, lag):
    rows = len(signal) - (dimension - 1) * lag
    return np.column_stack([
        signal[(dimension - 1 - j) * lag:(dimension - 1 - j) * lag + rows]
        for j in range(dimension)
    ])

Expert optional subtopic: a SW1PerS-style periodicity score
Sliding windows turn a scalar signal into a point cloud. Centre each window and normalise its length so that the calculation responds to shape rather than offset or amplitude. Compare a sinusoid with a chirp, whose frequency changes through time. Before running the cell, predict which cloud should have the stronger persistent \(H_1\) loop.

def forward_windows(signal, dimension, lag):
    rows = len(signal) - dimension * lag
    W = np.column_stack([signal[j*lag:j*lag+rows] for j in range(dimension+1)])
    W = W - W.mean(axis=1, keepdims=True)
    return W / np.maximum(np.linalg.norm(W, axis=1, keepdims=True), 1e-12)

title: Week 8 participant practical: choosing an advanced persistence framework
text:
This is the student investigation in choosing topology for genuinely changing systems. The core calculation follows a complex that gains and loses a loop. An expert extension reconstructs the Turner critical-value example and a two-generator transport matrix.
The core separates repeated persistence, correspondence, zigzag persistence, multiparameter persistence and vineyards by the maps each method requires.
Working rule. Run one section at a time. Before each TODO, state what shape, dimension or direction you expect in the output. Optional extensions come only after the core checkpoints agree.
Code
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
RNG=np.random.default_rng(3024)
def rank_mod2(A):
 A=np.array(A,dtype=np.uint8,copy=True)%2; row=rank=0
 for col in range(A.shape[1]):
  piv=np.flatnonzero(A[row:,col])
  if not len(piv): continue
  q=row+piv[0]; A[[row,q]]=A[[q,row]]
  for i in range(A.shape[0]):
   if i!=row and A[i,col]: A[i]^=A[row]
  row+=1; rank+=1
  if row==A.shape[0]: break
 return rank

title: Week 3 lecture walkthrough: Čech and Rips filtrations
Week 3 lecture walkthrough: Čech and Rips filtrations
text:
1. Observe: lecture demonstration
Presenter cue. Show the object before the calculation. Ask the room to separate what is given from what will be constructed.
The three points below form an equilateral triangle of side length \(1.9\). We examine radius \(r=1\). Pairwise balls intersect because every pair of centres is at distance below \(2r\). Before constructing a complex, ask the genuinely joint question: do all three balls share one point?

r=1.0
theta=np.linspace(0,2*np.pi,300)

for i,p in enumerate(triangle):
    ax.plot(p[0]+r*np.cos(theta),p[1]+r*np.sin(theta),alpha=.75)
    ax.scatter(*p); ax.text(p[0],p[1]+.08,str(i),ha='center')
ax.set_aspect('equal'); ax.set_title('Three radius-1 balls'); ax.axis('off'); plt.show()

print('smallest common enclosing radius:',round(enclosing_radius(triangle),3))

title: Week 3 lecture walkthrough: Čech and Rips filtrations
text:
2. Predict: lecture demonstration
Presenter cue. Pause here and collect at least two predictions before revealing any output.
Before running the construction:

Which vertices and edges should appear in both complexes at \(r=1\)?
Should the 2-simplex \((0,1,2)\) appear in Čech, Rips, both, or neither?
Predict \(\beta_1\) for the graph alone, the Čech complex, and the full Rips complex.
If \(r\) increases, can an existing simplex disappear from either filtration? Explain using the definition.

The code constructs simplices only through dimension 2. This is sufficient for \(H_0\) and \(H_1\), which are the quantities reported here; it is not sufficient for a valid \(H_2\) calculation because omitted 3-simplices could fill 2-cycles.
Worked prediction. All vertices and edges appear in both complexes. The triple has diameter \(1.9<2r\), so Rips fills it. Its smallest enclosing radius is \(1.9/\sqrt{3}\approx1.097>1\), so the three balls have no common intersection and Čech does not fill it. Therefore the graph and Čech complex have \(\beta_1=1\), while the Rips complex has \(\beta_1=0\). Increasing \(r\) can only add simplices.

title: Week 3 lecture walkthrough: Čech and Rips filtrations
text:
3. Implement: lecture demonstration
Reveal. Run one cell at a time. Name the domain, codomain, complex, module or summary before interpreting its values.
Čech records common intersections of balls. Rips checks only pairwise distances and fills every clique. The following calculation exposes the difference without calling a TDA library.


Code
C=cech(triangle,r); R=rips(triangle,r); G=graph_complex(triangle,r)
for name,K in [('graph',G),('Cech',C),('Rips',R)]:
 print(name,sorted(K,key=lambda s:(len(s),s)),'Betti',betti(K))


The 1-skeletons agree. The Rips rule adds the 2-simplex because its decision is completely determined by the three edges. Čech asks for a common intersection of all three balls, which is a stronger condition.

Check the filtration property


Code

print('violations:',valid_filtration_value(bad))
fixed=dict(bad); fixed[(0,1,2)]=max(fixed[f] for f in faces((0,1,2)))
print('repaired triangle value:',fixed[(0,1,2)],'violations:',valid_filtration_value(fixed))


The triangle cannot enter at \(1.2\) while its edge \((1,2)\) waits until \(1.4\). Assigning the maximum face value is the smallest repair. Equal filtration values are allowed: a simplex and some faces can enter together.


Follow one point cloud through scale


Code
angles=np.linspace(0,2*np.pi,8,endpoint=False); circle=np.c_[np.cos(angles),np.sin(angles)]
radii=[0.20,0.39,0.72,1.01]

plt.show()


At the smallest radius the vertices are separate. Once adjacent points connect, one graph cycle appears. Later, new diagonals create triangles that fill the central class. A Betti number at one chosen radius hides this evolution, which is why the nested family matters.

Scale is held fixed here. The difference comes entirely from what higher-order relation is inferred from the same three pairwise edges. A graph retains the cycle, Čech retains it because the balls lack a joint intersection, and Rips fills it by clique completion.

title: Week 3 lecture walkthrough: Čech and Rips filtrations
text:
5. Interpret: lecture demonstration
Presenter close. Ask what the example supports, what information was discarded and which stronger claim would be unjustified.

Rips fills every clique, while Čech requires a joint intersection. Pairwise overlap does not imply triple overlap.
For a good cover such as finite Euclidean balls and their non-empty intersections, the Nerve Theorem gives the nerve and union the same homotopy type.
A Rips complex contains a simplex for every clique, so the displayed proximity graph is only its 1-skeleton.
Clique filling treats mutual pairwise interaction as evidence of a coherent higher-order unit. This may or may not match the mechanism.
Euclidean distance may ignore periodic boundaries, anisotropic scales, observation functions, temporal order, or dynamically meaningful similarity.

◇ Object check. The observed object is a finite point cloud. The union of balls, its Čech nerve, the Rips clique complex, and their homology groups are four different constructed objects. A loop belongs to the selected construction, not automatically to the underlying dynamical system.

section: Optional extension: what ordinary persistence forgets about labels
text:
Optional extension: what ordinary persistence forgets about labels
The two panels below contain exactly the same point locations. Only the red/blue labels differ. Predict what ordinary Rips persistence will report after the labels are deleted. Then describe a chromatic question that distinguishes mixing from separation.


Code
angles = np.linspace(0, 2*np.pi, 96, endpoint=False)
radii = np.repeat([0.65, 1.0], 48)
theta = np.tile(angles[:48], 2)
label_cloud = np.c_[radii*np.cos(theta), radii*np.sin(theta)]
mixed = np.arange(96) % 2
separated = (radii > 0.8).astype(int)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8, 3.5))
for ax, labels, title in zip(axes, [mixed, separated], ['labels mixed', 'labels separated by ring']):
    ax.scatter(*label_cloud.T, c=np.where(labels, 'tab:blue', 'tab:red'), s=18)
    ax.set_title(title); ax.set_aspect('equal'); ax.axis('off')
plt.show()
